translations.text: The Jewish brothers in Jerusalem and in the land of Judea, to our Jewish brothers in Egypt: Greetings! Peace and grace be with you.
May God be good to you and remember his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants.
May he give you all a heart to fear him and carry out his commandments wholeheartedly and with a willing spirit.
May he open your ears and your hearts to his laws and his commandments, and establish peace with you.
May he hear your petition, be reconciled to you, and not abandon you in times of trouble.
And now, here we are, praying for you.

In the year 169, during the reign of Demetrius, we Jews wrote to you amid the distress and afflictions that befell us in these years, since Jason and those with him were sent from the kingdom to the holy land.
They burned the gates and shed innocent blood. We prayed and pleaded with the Lord, and he heard our voice. We offered sacrifices and fine flour, lit the lamps, and set out the bread of the Presence.
And now you are to celebrate the Festival of Shelters in December.

In the year 188. Those in Jerusalem and Judea, and all the elders of Judea, to Aristobulus, the teacher of King Ptolemy, who is descended from the anointed priests, and to the Jews in Egypt: Peace and good health!
We give abundant and heartfelt thanks to God, who stood by us and rescued us from all the afflictions that came upon us.
For when the king came against us in war to attack the holy city,

he drove him away and cast him into Persia. For when he went there with his entire army, he who was considered invincible was killed in the temple of Nanaea, whose priests cunningly seized them and shut them in.
For Antiochus and his friends had gone there as though he intended to live with her, in order to receive great wealth as a dowry.
Nanaea's priests conspired and made him a promise. But when he went inside the temple wall with a few men,
they opened a small door and came in upon him, threw stones at him and killed him, cut off his head, and threw it to those outside.
But blessed in everything is our God, who handed over the wicked.

Since we are about to celebrate the purification of the temple on the twenty-fifth of December, we wanted to inform you too, so that you also might celebrate it like the Festival of Shelters. We will also tell you about the fire, when Nehemiah built the temple and the altar and offered sacrifices.

When our ancestors were going to Persia, the righteous priests of that time secretly took some of the fire from the altar and hid it in a cistern that had no water. They concealed it so that no one would know its location.
After many years had passed, when it pleased God, Nehemiah was sent by the king of Persia with the descendants of those priests who had hidden the fire.

He sent them to bring fire. They returned and said that they had found no fire, but only murky water. He ordered them to take some of it and bring it. When the sacrifices and offerings had been brought up, Nehemiah ordered the priests to sprinkle some of it on the wood and the sacrifices.
When they had done this and a little time had passed, the sun began to shine, though it was obscured by clouds. Then a great fire blazed up, so that everyone was amazed.
The priests stood in prayer until the fire had finished its work. When the priests, Jonathan, and the rest came down, they said that it had blazed up through Nehemiah's prayer.
His prayer was as follows: “Lord, Lord, God, ruler of all and creator of everything, awesome and mighty, righteous and merciful, you alone are king, and you alone are kind,
you alone are the sustainer, righteous, living forever and ruling over all, Israel's deliverer from every evil, who chose our ancestors and made them holy.
Accept this offering on behalf of all your people Israel, and protect and sanctify your portion and your inheritance.
Gather our scattered people, free those enslaved among the unclean and despised nations, and look upon us, so that the nations may know that you are our God.
Punish those who exalt themselves and arrogantly enslave others.
Establish your people firmly in your holy place, as Moses said.
Meanwhile, the priests stood singing songs of praise.
When the sacrifices and offerings were completed, Nehemiah ordered them to set down the remaining water and surround the place with large stones.
When they did this, a flame of fire blazed until the light of the fire on the altar had died away.

When the matter became known and was disclosed to the king of Persia—that murky water had been found in the place where those taken captive had hidden the fire, and that Nehemiah and those with him had used it to consecrate the offerings and sacrifices—
The king built up the place and made a temple there after investigating the matter.
the king gave them great and valuable gifts. They, however, took them and gave them to those who were in need.
Nehemiah's people called it Gonaphthar, which means “purification,” but among many people it is called Nephthai.
It is found in the book of Jeremiah the prophet that he ordered those who came afterward to take fire, as it explains.

The prophet, who gave them the law, instructed those who came afterward not to forget the Lord's commandments or let their minds be turned aside when they saw idols of gold and silver and their adornment.
He said other things like these and urged them not to remove the law from their hearts.

It was also written in the book that, as it had been revealed to the prophet, he ordered the ark and the tabernacle to go with him. Then he went out to the mountain that Moses had climbed, where he had seen the Lord's inheritance.
Jeremiah came and found a chamber in a cave. He went inside, placed the tabernacle, the ark, and the incense altar there, and blocked the entrance.
Some of those who had gone with him went out to identify the path and the place, but they could not find them.
When Jeremiah learned of this, he rebuked them and said, “The place will not be known until God gathers the congregation of his people and has mercy on them.
Then the Lord will reveal these things, and the Lord's glory and the cloud will appear, as it used to appear to Moses, and as Solomon also asked that the place be greatly sanctified.”
It was also related that, in keeping with the wisdom he possessed, he offered offerings and sacrifices for the dedication and completion of the temple.
Just as Moses prayed to the Lord, and fire came down from heaven and consumed the sacrifices and offerings, so Solomon also prayed, and fire came down and consumed the sacrifices and burnt offerings.
For Moses had said, “Because the [?] of the sin offering was not eaten, the fire consumed it.”
Likewise, Solomon also observed eight days.

It was also related in the writings and memoirs of Nehemiah that he acted in this way: he collected and arranged the books of the kingdoms, of the prophets, and of David, and the kings' letters concerning offerings and sacrifices.
In the same way, Judas also gathered together everything that had been scattered because of the wars we experienced, and these things are here with us.
Therefore, if you need any of them, send for them and obtain them for yourselves.
Since we are about to celebrate the purification, we have also written to you so that you too may celebrate it.
Now God, who saved his people in every way and gave everyone an inheritance, kingship, priesthood, and holiness—

As he promised through the Law, we hope in him that he will soon have mercy on us and gather us from everywhere under heaven to his holy place. For he has rescued us from many evils and has also purified the place.
Now concerning Judas Maccabeus and his brothers, the purification of the great and glorious temple, and the rededication of the altar;
and also concerning the wars that took place against Antiochus Epiphanes and his son Eupator;

and concerning the wonders openly performed from heaven for those who fought bravely on behalf of the Jews, so that, although they were few in number, they pursued and scattered all the nations of the lands that came against them with arrogance and recklessness;

so that the temple and sanctuary, renowned throughout the earth, enjoyed peace and quiet, the city was freed from subjection to the nations, and they gathered and restored the laws that were close to being swept away, through the Lord’s will and his mercy toward them.
We have taken great pains to write a concise account in one book of all these events, which Jason of Cyrene recorded in five books.

For we saw the overwhelming abundance of material and the difficulty faced by those who wish to investigate the accounts of the events and the narration of so many matters, because of the length of the narrative.

We have taken pains to arrange it carefully and present it concisely, so that readers may truly find delight, those who wish to retain the account attentively may remember it easily, and its usefulness may be clearly apparent to everyone who reads it.

For our part, we took responsibility for these matters and wrote them in an abridged form. This was not easy for us. Rather, with sweat, toil, weariness, and much sleeplessness, we compared, arranged, and wrote them in an abridged form.

For just as someone who wishes to arrange and prepare a banquet and refreshment for many people does not find it easy himself, but gladly takes on toil and weariness because he wishes to refresh and please those he has invited, so we too, for the enjoyment and refreshment of many, have gladly taken on toil and weariness and endured great hardship.
We have therefore declined to write a full account of all the events, and instead wish, with diligence and great effort, to relate briefly what has been written and told at length.

For just as a master builder, when building a house, is concerned with the whole plan of the construction, while the one who paints and decorates it with colors inquires into and seeks out everything needed for the house’s decoration, so I think it is with us as well.
For examining and investigating everything and writing it all down together is required of the one who begins the work.
But pursuing brevity of expression and leaving out many details is permitted to someone who tells much in few words in an abridged account.

From here, then, let us begin the accounts mentioned earlier and put together in an abridged form. For it is good for someone to explain and persuade at length before the account, but to tell the account itself briefly.
When the holy city was living in quiet and peace, and the laws were being faithfully observed because of the righteousness of Onias the high priest and his hatred of evil,
even kings came to honor the temple and the place with honors and great and splendid offerings.
Thus Seleucus, king of Asia, provided from his own resources everything needed for the service of the sacrifices.
But Simon, who belonged to the tribe of Benjamin and had been appointed administrator of the temple, opposed the priests, for he supported the wrongdoing that was taking place in the city.
When he could not overcome Onias the high priest, he went to Apollonius son of Thraseas, who at that time was ruler and governor of Syria and Phoenicia.

He informed him about the treasury in the temple in Jerusalem and told him that the wealth in it was beyond measure or counting. He said that all this should not be assigned to the account for sacrifices and offerings, but should be under the king’s authority.

Apollonius went and informed the king about the treasury and the wealth of which he had been told. The king summoned Heliodorus, who had been put in charge of affairs, and commissioned and sent him to take and bring back all the treasure and wealth about which he had been told.
Heliodorus immediately set out and traveled through the cities of Syria and Phoenicia, hurrying to carry out and complete the king’s command.

When Heliodorus came to Jerusalem, he was received with great honor by the high priest and the city. He explained to them the matter on which he had been sent, which had been reported to the king, and asked them whether these things were really true.
The high priest explained to him that these were deposits held for orphans and widows,

and that some belonged to Hyrcanus son of Tobias, an honored and wealthy man. It was not as the wicked slanderer Simon had come and reported. The total amounted to four hundred talents of silver and two hundred of gold.

Those who had trusted in the holiness of the place, the integrity of the temple, and its great and glorious reputation throughout the world—that it would not be plundered or robbed—could not be wronged and deprived of their possessions.
But Heliodorus, because of the king’s command, insisted that these funds must be brought into the royal treasury and deposited there.
He appointed a day for them when he would enter, inspect them, and take possession of them. There was no small distress throughout the whole city.
The priests, in their priestly robes, threw themselves on the ground, crying out and pleading with the one who had given them the law that deposits should be kept completely safe for their owners.
The hearts of everyone who saw the high priest melted, for the appearance of his face and his changed expression revealed the anguish of his soul.
For grace and beauty of appearance had been poured over the man and rested upon his body, and because of this the painful suffering within his soul became evident.
People also came out of their houses in crowds, pleading and praying that the temple would not become an object of ridicule and mockery.

Women, with sackcloth tied around their waists, wandered distractedly through the streets. Of the young women who had been kept indoors, some ran to the doorways, some to the wall, and others peered out through the windows.
They all stretched out their hands, crying out and pleading with the one who dwells in heaven.
It was a sight to move anyone to compassion: the anguish and distress of the people, and the struggle, suffering, and anxious expectation of the high priest.
They all cried out and pleaded with God Almighty that the things entrusted to those who had received them in trust would be kept completely safe, with every care.
But Heliodorus was pressing ahead to accomplish the business for which he had come.

He began to enter the treasury with the armed men and attendants who were with him. Immediately the Lord of spirits, the God of all power and all authority, appeared and gave them a wonder and a great revelation, so that all who had dared to enter lost their strength and fell down in amazement at the power of God that had appeared to them.

For a terrifying horse appeared to them, ridden by a man exceedingly handsome in appearance and splendid in the garments he wore. He came charging, causing a commotion before Heliodorus with the clattering sound of his armor. Its rider appeared to be equipped with golden armor.

Two other young men also appeared with him, handsome in appearance, magnificent in strength, and splendid and astonishing in their clothing. They stood on either side of Heliodorus and flogged him with heavy blows.
Suddenly he fell to the ground, enveloped in deep darkness, and they picked him up and carried him outside into the courtyard.
The man who a little earlier had been entering the treasury with arrogance and great power now lay powerless, unable to help himself. The power of God had been plainly revealed.
He lay there, incapacitated by the working of truth, with neither hope nor expectation of life.

But the people blessed the Lord, who had brought glory to his place. The temple, which a little earlier had been full of trembling and terror, was filled with delight and joy through the action and revelation of the Lord Almighty.
Immediately some of Heliodorus's friends approached Onias and begged him to pray and plead with the Lord to grant life to the man who lay there utterly without hope.
The high priest considered that the king might perhaps suppose that something had happened to Heliodorus through some action by the Jews, so he offered sacrifices for the man's life.

While the high priest stood making atonement for him, those same young men appeared again to Heliodorus in the same clothing as before. They said to him, “Be deeply grateful to Onias the high priest, for it is because of him that the Lord has granted you life.
As for you, who have been scourged by God, go and proclaim to everyone his greatness and his mighty dominion.” When they had said these things to him, they were no longer seen.
Heliodorus offered sacrifices to God and pleaded and prayed earnestly before him, who had granted him life. He also honored Onias greatly, and then returned to the king with his entire force.
He testified and told everyone about the deeds and power of the mighty God who had appeared to him before his own eyes.
The king questioned Heliodorus about what had happened and wanted to send someone to Jerusalem again. Heliodorus said to him,

“If you have someone who is guilty before you and hostile to your interests, send him there. You will receive him back flogged and tortured, if he even survives, because the power of God truly is in that place.”
For he whose dwelling is in heaven is the one who watches over and guards that place, and he torments, scourges, and destroys those who come to harm it.
This is how matters stood concerning Heliodorus and the protection of the treasury.

But that wicked Simon, whom we mentioned earlier as the informer and betrayer of the city and the treasury, was slandering Onias and bringing accusations against him, claiming that he had brought about what had happened to Heliodorus and was responsible for all the troubles that had come upon him.
He dared to say that the man who had benefited his city, cared for his fellow citizens, and zealously upheld the law was responsible for all these evils.
The evil of his hostility grew so great that many murders were committed by those whom Simon himself incited.
So Onias saw the malicious jealousy, and saw Apollonius, the ruler and governor of Syria and Phoenicia, stirring up trouble, supporting Simon, and adding to his wickedness.
It even reached the king’s ears that he was a slanderer and betrayer of his fellow citizens. Onias therefore considered and reflected on how help might come to his people.

He understood and saw that he had no further means of bringing about peace unless God’s mercy willed it, that matters could not be set right without God, and that Simon would not cease his wickedness and troublemaking unless help came from heaven.

After King Seleucus died and Antiochus, called Epiphanes, succeeded him as king, Jason, the brother of Onias the high priest, acted deceitfully and obtained authority over the high priesthood from the king.
He promised to give him 360 talents of silver, and another eighty talents from other revenues.

He also promised to give another 150 if the king would allow him to build a gymnasium in Jerusalem according to Greek custom, establish a wrestling competition in which people would compete in the stadium, and register the inhabitants of Jerusalem as Antiochenes.
When the king gave him permission and he wickedly seized the high priesthood and leadership through injustice, he immediately turned all his people toward a pagan way of thinking.

He also removed and abolished the provisions granted to the Jews through God’s mercy, which had been secured through John, the father of Eupolemus, who had gone as an envoy to the Romans concerning peace. He dismantled the true religious practices and laws, and established and introduced wicked laws and customs.
For he diligently and hastily established a gymnasium beneath the city wall, subjected those who were physically strong, and brought them under a prescribed measure.
Such was the zeal for paganism, the folly of Greek ways, and the error of the nations brought about by Jason, that wicked man who was no high priest. Impurity increased so greatly

that the priests no longer cared about the service of the altar, the sacrifices, or the offerings. Instead, they despised the temple and its service and hurried to watch and enjoy the unlawful wrestling and the [?] of combat in the arena.
They despised the honor of their ancestors’ worship and desired the empty glory of pagan practices.

For this reason disaster overtook them. Those whose practices they had envied, and whom they had wanted to imitate in everything, turned against them and became their enemies. At their hands they were punished according to their deeds.
For it is neither good nor right for anyone to act unjustly against the holy laws. But in due time each day makes these things known.
When the athletic competition was held at Tyre, as it was once every five years, the king also came there to watch.

The abominable and unclean Jason sent spectators from Jerusalem who were Antiochenes, and sent with them 3,300 in silver to bring for the sacrifice offered there to Heracles. But those carrying the money requested and urged that it should not be used for the sacrificial service, because that was not right, and they assigned it to expenses for other matters.
Thus, although the sender had sent it for this purpose, because of those who urged that it be handled this way, it was put to ordinary use for another service.

When Apollonius son of Menestheus was sent to Egypt to present special honors to Philometor, king of Egypt, Antiochus concluded that Philometor was hostile to the affairs of his kingdom and took precautions for his own safety. For this reason he came to Joppa on business and went up from there to Jerusalem.
He was received with exceptional honor and praise by Jason and the city, with acclaim and shouting. Afterward he set out from there for Phoenicia.
After three years, Jason sent Menelaus, the brother of the wicked Simon, to deliver to the king the gifts he had promised him and to speak to him about other important matters that concerned them.
But when he went, he presented himself before the king and praised himself. He asked for the high priesthood, outbidding Jason by giving three hundred additional talents of silver.
After receiving the king’s authorization, he returned. He did nothing worthy of the high priesthood, but was clothed in fury and anger and was full of wild and reckless thoughts.
As for Jason, who had plotted against his brother, another man now plotted against him, and he fled to the land of Ammon.
Menelaus held office, but he did not have the means to pay what he had promised the king.

Sostratus, who had been appointed governor of the citadel, came and demanded payment from him, for he had been given authority to collect the additional revenues. Because of this, both of them were summoned before the king.
Menelaus left his brother Lysimachus as high priest in his place, while Sostratus left Crates, who was in charge of the Cypriots.
While they were occupied with these matters, the people of Tarsus and Mallus happened to revolt because Antioch had been given as a gift to the king’s concubine.
When the king heard, he quickly came to pacify them, leaving Andronicus there as his deputy, the man who had been placed in charge of important affairs.

Menelaus, thinking that he had found an opportunity, stole some of the temple’s gold vessels and gave them to Andronicus. It was discovered that he had sent the rest away and sold them in Tyre and the surrounding towns.
When Onias learned this for certain, he rebuked him, then withdrew and went to Daphne, which is beside Antioch.

Because of this, Menelaus went secretly to Andronicus and asked him to kill Onias. Andronicus came to Onias and deceitfully spoke words of peace to him. With oaths and persuasion, he pledged his right hand and persuaded him to come out of the sanctuary. Onias came out, though he was doubtful in his mind. As soon as he came out, Andronicus killed him, showing no respect for his righteousness.
Because of this, not only the Jews were denouncing and reviling him, but many of the Gentiles were also insulting and reviling him over the unjust killing of the man.

When the king returned from the regions of Cilicia, the Jews in all the cities complained to him about the injustice committed in the killing of Onias. Many Gentiles also supported them, for they were deeply distressed that Onias had been killed without a trial.
When King Antiochus heard this, he was grieved to his very soul and wept bitterly. He was utterly overcome with sorrow over the death of a man who was righteous, chaste, humble, peaceable, and kind.

He became fiercely angry and ordered that Andronicus be stripped of his purple robes, that his clothes be torn, and that he be led around the whole city. At the very place where he had wronged Onias, he killed that wicked man. Thus the Lord repaid him with the punishment he deserved.

The people of Jerusalem gathered within the city against Lysimachus, with Menelaus’s approval, and demanded from him the large amount of gold he had taken. When the news spread abroad, many came against Lysimachus.

When Lysimachus saw that the crowds were growing and becoming angry with him, he armed about three thousand men and began killing with his wicked hands. His assistant and the leader of the killers was an impure and abominable man, advanced in years and very deranged in his thinking.
When they saw Lysimachus’s deceitfulness and wickedness, they took stones and clubs, and some took ashes, and threw those who were with Lysimachus and his supporters into terror and confusion.
They struck down many of them dead and knocked some to the ground, while the rest fled. They killed the plunderer of the temple himself beside the treasury.
Over these matters, Menelaus stood against them in court.
When the king came to Tyre, the three men sent by the elders of the assembly presented their case before him.
When Menelaus saw that he was being defeated, he promised Ptolemy many gifts to persuade the king.
Ptolemy took the king aside, separating him from them for a little while as though to let him rest, and changed his mind.

He acquitted Menelaus, who was the cause of all these evils, of his accusers’ charges. But he condemned to death those unfortunate, helpless men who would have been acquitted as innocent even if they had pleaded their case before the Scythians.
Immediately the citizens promised to pay the unjust expenses on behalf of the city, the people, and the priestly vessels.
For this reason even the people of Tyre were deeply distressed over the unjust sentence by which these men had been put to death for no reason. The Tyrians took them and buried them with great honor.
Menelaus sent to demand the payment for the injustice that he had promised. He grew more arrogant and stronger in his wickedness, and became a great adversary of his fellow citizens.
At this same time Antiochus went to Egypt for the second time.
It happened that throughout the city, for about forty days, horsemen were seen racing through the air, dressed in golden robes, holding spears, and equipped with every kind of weapon.

They were spurring their horses and charging here and there, brandishing their shields and drawing their swords. Their bows were drawn, and they were dressed in armor and equipped with every kind of golden weapon for battle. All of them together shone and flashed.
All the people pleaded and prayed that this vision would turn out for good.

A false report spread that Antiochus had died. Jason took about a thousand men and came and attacked the city without warning. He pressed the attack fiercely against the city, and most of the people fled and went up onto the wall, because the city was close to destruction. Menelaus fled and went up into the citadel.

Jason slaughtered his fellow citizens. The wicked man did not consider or understand that his joy was full of distress and great mourning, because he was making war and committing murder among his own people and his own kindred.
Although he did all these things, he could not seize power. Instead, his undertaking ended in disgrace, and he gave up and fled again to the land of Ammon.

His final end was evil and bitter. Aretas, king of the Arabs, plotted against him, and he escaped from there and fled from city to city. Everyone pursued him as a rebel against the law, and they despised and scorned him as a betrayer of his city and his people. In great disgrace he fled to Egypt.

Like refuse thrown out of a house, he was thrown out of his own country, and he perished in Lacedaemon, in a foreign land. He had gone there to seek shelter among people he regarded as his own kindred, and he died there.
He was not granted burial in his ancestors’ tomb, or weeping, or mourning, or any of the honors with which people are buried.

They sent word to the king about everything that had happened. He thought that Judea intended to rebel, so he hurried back from Egypt, filled with anger and fury, and killed many people in the city with the sword.
He ordered his soldiers to kill without mercy everyone who fell into their hands. They even entered the houses and killed people.
There was slaughter of old men, boys, young men, and young women, and destruction of sons, daughters, and little infants.
Thus, in three days about eighty thousand people were lost and destroyed: forty thousand were killed, and forty thousand were sold into slavery.
All this was not enough for the king. He also dared to enter the great and holy temple, renowned throughout the earth. His guide was Menelaus, who had become a betrayer of the law and of his country.

With his unclean hands he took the sacred vessels, including those given by other kings and those deposited by cities for the glory, magnificence, and honor of the temple. He took everything in its sanctuary and all its treasures with his defiled hands and handed them over.

Antiochus became proud and boastful in his thinking. He did not consider or understand that, because of the sins of the city’s inhabitants, the Lord had been angry for a little while and had withdrawn his watchful care from the place.

For if they had not been caught up in many sins, they would not have suffered and endured these things. It would have been as when Heliodorus was sent by King Seleucus concerning the treasure in the treasury: when he tried to enter the treasury, a bitter scourge was sent against him, and he returned humbled from his lofty thinking.
For the people did not exist for the sake of the place; rather, the Lord chose the place for the sake of the people.

For this reason the place itself shared with the people in the punishment for their wickedness. Later, when deliverance came from the Lord, it also shared in the blessings. The temple, which had been abandoned in God’s anger, was restored again in great glory through the favor of the Most High.

Antiochus took eighteen hundred talents from the temple and hurried away to Antioch. In his arrogance he thought he could turn the land into sea and the sea into dry land, because he had become exceedingly proud and boastful in his thinking.
He left governors who mistreated our people. In Jerusalem he left Philip, a Phrygian by birth, whose disposition was unclean, tyrannical, and abominable—worse than the man who had left him there.

And in Gerizim, Andronicus. With them he left Menelaus, who was even more arrogant and conceited than they were and mistreated the people of his own city. Antiochus was filled with anger and bitter hostility toward the Jews.
He sent Apollonius, the leader of all the unclean, with an army of twenty-two thousand, ordering them to kill those who were old and advanced in years and to sell the women and young people.
When this man came to Jerusalem, he deceitfully spoke words of peace to them and waited until the holy Sabbath day. When he found the Jews resting, he armed everyone who was with him.
He ordered them to kill everyone who came outside the city as if to watch a spectacle. He also rushed into the city, armed along with his army, and killed many people.

But Judas Maccabeus withdrew with nine others who were with him and went into the wilderness. They lived like wild animals in the mountains, sustaining themselves on roots and the plants of the ground so that they would not share in the defilement.

A short time afterward, the king sent another man, an Athenian, to compel the Jews to transgress the laws and commandments of their ancestors and not to conduct their lives according to the laws of God.

They were also to defile the temple in Jerusalem and name it the temple of Baalshamin Olympius, and the one in Gerizim, in keeping with the inhabitants of that region, the temple of Baalshamin Xenios.
The distress and oppression that all of them suffered were terrible and bitter.

For the temple was filled with the revelry, music, and celebrations of the Gentiles, and they treated it with great contempt. They also had sexual relations with women all around it, and they brought forbidden things inside the temple.
The altar, which had been prepared for the offerings prescribed in the law, was entirely filled with pollution and uncleanness.
The oppression was so severe that no one could observe the Sabbath or celebrate and keep an ancestral festival, or even acknowledge and say that he was a Jew.

Every month, on the days celebrating the king's birth, they were brought under bitter compulsion to offer sacrifices. There was also a festival of Dionysus, and they compelled them to carry branches, go around in procession, and take part in the festivities on the day of Dionysus.
He also sent an order to the neighboring Gentile cities and to Ptolemy that they should compel the Jews in the same way, but show mercy to those who obeyed them and did what they wanted.
Those who were unwilling to turn to pagan beliefs were to be killed. Anyone who saw the people's grief and humiliation would be brokenhearted.

For they brought forward two women who had circumcised their sons. They hung their sons at their breasts and paraded the women throughout the city. Finally, they took them up and threw them from the wall.

Others fled and secretly went into caves to observe the Sabbath there. People came and informed Philip, and they went and burned them because they were afraid to defend themselves on the glorious Sabbath day.

Therefore I ask all who read this book not to be afraid, alarmed, or shaken by what has happened to us. Instead, consider that the judgment that came upon us was not for the destruction of our people, but for their discipline.
For this too is a sign of great kindness: they were not left for a long time to act wickedly, but fell under many punishments.
For the Lord has not treated us as he treats other nations, patiently waiting until their sins reach their full measure and finally repaying them with torment.
Instead, he punishes us now so that he will not torment us at the end.
For this reason, he has never withdrawn his mercy from us. He does indeed discipline us with punishments, but he has not abandoned his people.
But what has been said up to this point is enough as a reminder. Let us now return to the narrative.
Eleazar, the chief of the scribes, an old man whose face was pleasing and very handsome, was being compelled to eat pork.
But he preferred a death by torment full of glory to living a short time in disgrace. He approached gladly and handed himself over to afflictions and tortures.
This is how steadfast people ought to surrender themselves rather than defile themselves by eating anything forbidden, because of the life and hope awaiting them.

Those whom the king had appointed over the interrogations and unjust floggings took the honored Eleazar aside privately, because they had known him for a long time. They urged him to bring sacrificial meat of a kind suitable for him, prepared for him, and eat it, but to make a pretense and give in by saying that he had eaten sacrificial meat in accordance with the king's command.
so that by doing this he might be spared death, and mercy might be shown him because of their longstanding friendship with him.

But he resolved on a courageous and noble course, worthy of his old age, his honorable years, his learning, and the godly discipline he had followed from childhood. He answered, “Quickly, without delay, lead me away and send me to Sheol.”
“For it would not be fitting at my age to act deceitfully and pretend. Many young people would say that Eleazar, a man ninety years old, had turned to paganism.
“Because of my pretense, and for the sake of my brief remaining life, they would go astray and perish, while I would become an object of disgrace, ridicule, mockery, and contempt in my old age.
“Even if I wished to escape this temporary death inflicted by human beings, I could not escape the hands of God, either in life or in death.
“Therefore, by departing this world courageously and bravely, I will bring my old age the honor it deserves.

“I will leave the young an example of bravery and courage, and encourage them to surrender themselves gladly to affliction, torture, and death for the sake of the pure, holy, and glorious law.” When he had said this, they immediately took him away and brought him to be tortured and afflicted.
Those who a little earlier had acted as his friends turned hostile because of these words of his, for they thought he had spoken them arrogantly and boastfully. They began to flog him.

When he was close to dying under the lashes, he groaned and said, “It is clear to the Lord, who possesses holy knowledge, that although I could escape this death, here I am enduring affliction, lashes, and bodily pain. Yet in my soul I rejoice that I endure these things for the sake of his law and the fear of him.”

After saying these things, he departed from this world. By his death he left not only the young but also many of the people an example and demonstration of courage and strength, and a glorious memory and remembrance.

It also happened that seven brothers were arrested with their mother. The king tried to force them to eat unclean pork, and whips and all kinds of instruments of torture and torment were brought and placed before them.
One of them, who was their leader, answered the king, “What are you asking to learn from us? We are ready to die rather than transgress the law of our ancestors.”
When the king heard this, he became very angry and ordered a frying pan and cauldrons to be heated.

When they had heated them intensely, he ordered them to cut out the tongue of the one who was their leader and cut off the extremities of all his limbs, while his mother and brothers stood watching him.

After they had mutilated all his limbs, he ordered them to bring him and throw him, still alive, onto the frying pan over the fire. As a strong smell of burning rose from his body, his brothers and their mother urged one another to die bravely.
“Look, the Lord God sees and truly has compassion on us, as Moses said in his song: ‘He has compassion on his servants.’”

When the first had died and departed this world, they brought the second to be mocked and flogged. They threw him down and stripped the hair from his head along with the skin. They asked him whether he would eat before his whole body was mutilated.
But he answered in the language of his ancestors, “I will not eat.” So they killed him too with the same torture.
When he was close to death, he said, “You wicked man, you are releasing us from this temporary life, but the King of the ages, for whose law we are dying, will raise us to everlasting life.”
After this they brought the third brother, mocking and torturing him. He ordered them to cut out his tongue. Immediately he put out his tongue and gladly stretched out his hands as well.
He answered courageously, “I received these from the one who dwells in heaven. For the sake of his law I gladly surrender them, and I hope to receive them back from him again.”
The king himself and those with him were amazed at the young man’s courage, since he did not show the slightest fear or concern about the lashes and tortures.
When this one had died, they brought the fourth, and they afflicted and tortured him too.

When he was close to death, he answered, “Death under torture at human hands is preferable because of the hope of resurrection to life from God in the world to come. But for you there will be no resurrection to life.”
When this one had died, they brought the fifth and flogged and afflicted him.

He looked at the king and said to him, “You have authority over human beings, and although you yourself are mortal, you do whatever you please. But do not suppose that our people have been abandoned by God.
“Wait, and you will see the sovereign power of his greatness, and how he will torment you and your descendants afterward.”

After this they brought forward the sixth. When he was near death, he spoke and said, “Do not deceive yourself for nothing. We are suffering these things on our own account, because we have sinned against our God. For this reason we have become a marvel of praise.
But do not think that you will prevail, since you have chosen to stand against God.”

Their mother was especially praiseworthy and deserving of remembrance and a blessed memorial. Although she saw all seven of her sons perish in a single day, she endured it joyfully because of the hope awaiting her with the Lord.

She pleaded with each one of them, saying in the language of their ancestors, “My son, have pity on me.” She was filled with a courageous spirit, and with fervor she stirred her womanly thoughts to a man’s resolve. As she pleaded with them, she said to them, “My sons,
I do not know how you appeared in my womb. It was not I who gave you life and breath, nor was it I who fashioned the form and appearance of each of you.

Rather, the Creator of the world, who formed the generations of humanity and searches all their intentions and thoughts, will himself give you breath and life again in his mercy, because you have handed over your bodies to destruction for the sake of his holy laws.”

When Antiochus saw that he was being scorned and despised by the voice of the woman who was reproaching him, he ignored it and acted as though he had not heard. While the young man stood there, he not only pleaded with him and tried to persuade him with words, but also swore many oaths to him: if he would obey him and turn away from the convictions of his ancestors, he would make him very wealthy, make him his friend, and entrust him with the affairs of the kingdom.
But when the young man paid no attention and was not taken in by his words, the king called his mother and urged her to advise her son so that he would not die.
After he had said a great deal to her, she said, “I will persuade him.”

She fell at her son’s feet and pleaded with him, while mocking the loathsome tyrant. In the language of their ancestors she said to him, “My son, have pity on me, who carried you in my womb for nine months, nursed you for three years, raised you, and brought you to this stage of life.
I beg you, my son, look at heaven and earth and everything in them. Consider and see that God made them from what did not exist. The human race also came into being in this way.

So do not be afraid of this condemned man. Instead, prove yourself worthy of your brothers and accept death, so that through the mercy that will again be shown to you, I may receive you again with your brothers.”
While she stood there pleading with him, the young man spoke and said, “What are you waiting for? I will not obey the king’s command. I obey the law of our ancestors that was given through Moses.
But you, who have devised and committed so many evils against the Hebrews, will not escape God’s hands.
For we are suffering these things because of our sins.
Our Lord God has been angry with us for a short time to rebuke and discipline us, but he will again be reconciled to his servants.
But you, wicked, unclean, and most loathsome of all people, do not exalt yourself or boast over God’s servants with empty hope.
For you will not escape the judgment of God, who rules over all.

For my brothers, who endured a brief, momentary affliction, will be with him in the life of light, in the glory of God’s kingdom. But you, by God’s just judgment, will receive the repayment your deeds deserve.

Like my brothers, I hand over my life and body for the sake of the law of our ancestors. I ask God to be reconciled soon and forgive our people, and that you may be called to account through torments and sufferings and acknowledge that he alone is God.
And may the wrath of the Most High, which has justly come upon our whole people, come to rest with me and my brothers.”
When the king heard these things, he became very angry and afflicted and tortured him more severely and bitterly than his brothers.
But he departed from the world undefiled, trusting completely in the Lord.
Last of all, their mother also died.
This is enough to say about the interrogations, tortures, and great and severe floggings.

Judas Maccabeus and those with him secretly entered the villages and gathered their fellow countrymen and those who had remained faithful to the law of Judaism. They assembled and numbered about six thousand men.
They were asking the Lord to look upon the people who were being trampled by many, and also to have mercy on the temple that had been defiled by the wicked.
They asked him also to rescue the city that was being destroyed and was close to becoming a wilderness, and to look again upon those who had been killed, whose blood had been poured out for nothing.
They asked him also to remember the innocent children who had perished unjustly, and, because of the blasphemies spoken against his name, to rise against them in fierce anger.

When Maccabeus and the company with him became firmly established and strong, he spread fear and dread of himself among all the nations. For God's anger was turning away and becoming mercy toward them.
He would enter unexpectedly and destroy cities and villages. He seized the nearby regions, won battles, and killed many.
He attacked especially at night and crushed many, and his courage was spoken of and became famous everywhere.

When Philip saw that Maccabeus was becoming increasingly powerful and renowned, and was victorious in all his battles, he wrote and sent word to Ptolemy, the chief official and governor of Syria and Phoenicia, asking him to support the king's interests.

Ptolemy immediately gave orders to Nicanor son of Patroclus, who was one of his leading Friends, and sent him with about twenty thousand troops to go and wipe out the entire Jewish people. He also sent Gorgias with him, a commander and leader experienced in warfare.
Nicanor had promised and pledged to the king that he would bring two thousand talents into the royal treasury from the sale of Jewish captives.

He immediately sent word to the city on the seacoast and invited its people to come and buy the Jews. He promised to give ninety people for one talent, without considering or anticipating the judgment of God Almighty that was about to overtake him.
People came and informed Judas of Nicanor's approach and told him about the entire army with him.
When the Jews heard this, many of them became afraid, doubted God's righteous judgment, and began fleeing in every direction.
Others were selling what they had left. All of them together were asking the Lord to rescue them from the hands of the wicked Nicanor, who had sold them before he had even come and seen them.

They asked this even if not for their own sake, then for the sake of the covenant he had made with their ancestors, and for the sake of his great, holy, and glorious name that had been invoked over them.

Judas Maccabeus gathered those with him, numbering six thousand men. He appealed to them and encouraged them not to fear battle or become alarmed and shaken by the great number of nations that had come against them unjustly.

He said to them, “Look and see the disgrace unjustly inflicted on the holy place by their hands. Give yourselves to the struggle and fight bravely.” He also reminded them of the disgrace and mockery that the city had suffered at their hands, and of their abolition of the ancestral laws.

He told them, “They trust in weapons and bodily strength, but we trust in the Lord our God, the Almighty, who has the power to overthrow not only our enemies but also the whole world with the breath of his mouth.”

He also reminded them of the deliverances their ancestors had experienced in their own times, and of the deliverance in the days of Sennacherib, when one hundred and eighty-five thousand had perished.

He also reminded them of the battle with the Galatians: how they had attacked them fiercely with eighty thousand troops, together with another forty thousand Macedonians who had come to assist them; and how they had gone out against them with a small force and defeated them because of the help from heaven that was with them.
When they heard these things, they were encouraged, strengthened, and emboldened, and courageously committed themselves to their law and their country. He divided the army into four divisions.
He appointed his brothers Simon, Joseph, and Jonathan as commanders and leaders over the separate divisions, entrusting fifteen hundred men to each of them.

He also instructed Eleazar to read the holy law to the people and gave them “God's help” as the watchword of deliverance. He himself was commander and leader of the first division, and he began to engage Nicanor in battle.

God Almighty became their helper from heaven, and he killed about nine thousand of them. They cut off the hands, blinded the eyes, and mutilated the limbs of a great many of their troops. Those who remained of their entire army fled.
They took all the wealth of those who had come to buy them. They pursued them a long way and then turned back because they were in a hurry,
for the time of Sabbath eve was approaching. For this reason they did not continue pursuing them.

They plundered and took everything the enemy had with them, including their weapons, and returned to observe the Sabbath. They gave thanks and greatly praised the Lord, who had delivered them that day and had begun to show them mercy.
After the Sabbath, they distributed some of their plunder to the sick, the poor, the orphans, and the widows. They divided the rest among themselves and the young men with them.
After doing this, they all cried out and prayed before the merciful Lord, asking him to remain gracious to his servants to the end.

Then Timothy and Bacchides attacked them again, and they killed more than thirty thousand of their men. They conquered and captured great, strong fortresses, took a great deal of plunder, and distributed it. They gave shares to the orphans, widows, and poor among the people, and also to the elderly.
They took and gathered all their weapons and stored them in designated places. The rest of the plunder they brought to Jerusalem, to the leaders of the people.
Timothy’s men had killed a certain wicked man who had caused the Jews great distress.

When they returned to their own land, they celebrated their victory in battle. They brought Callisthenes and those with him and burned them in a single house, because they had burned the holy gates and fled. They received punishment fitting their evil and unjust deeds.
Now the guilty and unclean Nicanor, who had brought a thousand merchants with him to buy the Jews,

was humbled and fell before those whom he had thought inferior to himself, through the power and help of God, who was with them. He abandoned his splendid clothing and fled like a slave to Antioch, in distress and great shame because of the destruction of his army.

He who had promised the Romans that he would pay them tribute from the captives of Jerusalem now proclaimed and said that the Jews had God as their helper, and that for this reason they could not be defeated, because they followed his commandments.
At that very time, King Antiochus happened to be returning from Persia in shame and great frustration.

For he had gone down to the place called the city of Persia, intending to capture the city and plunder the temple of idols that was there. But when the inhabitants of that country saw this, they gathered against him in great strength and defeated the entire army with him. When he saw that he had been defeated, he turned back in shame with his whole army.
As Antiochus was approaching Batnan, they informed him of what had happened to Nicanor and Timothy.

When he heard, he became furious and was greatly carried away by his anger. He intended to come and make the Jews pay for everything that had been done to him in Persia. He ordered his charioteer to drive with great haste so that he could arrive quickly. He said, “I will uproot Jerusalem, the city of the Jews, and make it a dwelling place for the nations.”

Immediately the judgment of the Lord, the mighty God of Israel, overtook him and struck him with a bitter, unseen affliction. Before he had finished speaking, a bitter and severe pain seized his internal organs and intestines.
He justly repaid the man who had tortured and tormented the internal organs of others with pain, suffering, and many tortures.

Although all these things had happened to him, he still raged and remained arrogant in his thinking. He was filled with anger that blazed like fire against the Jews, and he ordered his charioteer to drive still faster and more urgently. In the violent rush of his chariot, he was thrown out and suffered a severe and painful fall, and all his limbs were broken.

The man who only a little earlier had thought he could command even the waves of the sea, because his arrogance exceeded that of all other people, and could bring down all the lofty mountains, now lay on the ground, plainly displaying God’s power to everyone.

The wicked man’s suffering was so severe that worms even swarmed from his body. While he was still alive, his flesh fell away from him, and his body gave off such a foul smell that no one in his army could endure it.
The man who only a little earlier had thought he could command even the stars of heaven could now have no one approach him because of his foul smell.
From that point he began to abandon his excessive arrogance. Humbled, he turned toward knowledge of the truth, because he was being tormented and afflicted with every kind of scourge from heaven.
Unable to endure his own smell, he spoke and said, “It is right for a person to submit to God, and not, being mortal, to entertain thoughts against God.”
The wicked man prayed and pleaded with the Lord, who would no longer have mercy on him, saying:
“The holy city, which I was hurrying to go and overthrow and make a dwelling place for all the nations, I will rebuild and fortify.

And concerning the Jews he said, “I had intended that they should not even receive burial, but should become food for the birds of the sky and the wild animals of the earth, together with their wives and children. I will make them all Athenians.

“The holy temple, which I plundered before, I will adorn and embellish with every kind of decoration. I will provide sacred vessels many times over, and I will pay from my own resources every expense for sacrifices and offerings.
“After these things, I myself will also become a Jew, and wherever I go I will proclaim the greatness of God’s dominion.”
Despite all these things, he found no relief from his pains, for God's righteous judgment had overtaken him. When he despaired of his own life, he wrote the Jews the following letter of supplication.
“Antiochus, king and governor, to the worthy Jews, my fellow citizens: greetings and peace.”
May you and your children enjoy good health. I pray and ask this of God in heaven, in whom I place my hope because of his great kindness.

When I became ill, I remembered your interests, intending to grant you honor and great relief, for my heart burned with love for you from the time I set out from the land of Persia. When I was close to arriving, I fell into a severe and bitter illness, and I thought it best to attend to your interests above everything else.
For I do not know what will happen to me, but I hope to recover from this illness.
I observed that my father too, whenever he went up to the upper regions, used to make known who would succeed him,
so that, if something unfortunate happened, the people of the country would know who was appointed and would not fight one another.

So when I saw the nobles of my kingdom standing ready for the kingdom and waiting to see what would happen, I announced and appointed my son Antiochus as king. He is the one whom I entrusted to you many times when I went up to the upper regions. I have also written to him what is written here.
I ask and urge you to remember my kindness toward you, and for all of you together, and each one of you individually, to maintain friendship and brotherhood with my son.
For I know that he agrees with my intentions in everything and will treat you with gentleness and friendship.

But Antiochus, the murderer, the wicked man, and the blasphemer, died among the mountains in a foreign land, amid afflictions, torments, and great suffering, just as he himself had inflicted suffering on others.

Philip, the son of those who had raised him, took his body to bring it back with him. But as he was about to return, he became afraid of his son Antiochus and fled to Ptolemy, the son of Philometor, in Egypt.
Maccabeus and those with him, with the help of the Lord who was with them, took possession of the temple and the city.
They demolished the shrines and the idol temple that the Gentiles had built in its streets.

They purified the temple and made another altar. They passed stones through fire and took fire from them, and offered sacrifices and offerings after an interval of two years. They also prepared lamps, lampstands, incense, and the bread of the Presence.

After doing this, they fell facedown and prayed, asking the Lord that they might never again experience these afflictions and torments. Even if they should happen to sin, they asked to be disciplined mercifully by him himself, and not to be handed over to uncircumcised, unclean, and blasphemous Gentiles.
It happened that the temple was purified again on the very same day on which it had been defiled by the nations: the twenty-fifth of the month called December.

With joy and great rejoicing, they celebrated an eight-day festival every year, like the Festival of Booths. They remembered that only a short time before, during the Festival of Booths, they had been living in mountains and caves and grazing like animals.
For this reason they held palm branches and praised and thanked the one who had delivered them and given them strength to cleanse and consecrate his place.
They all agreed together that the entire congregation of the Jews should observe these days every year.
Such was the end and death of Antiochus, who was called Epiphanes.
Now let us also speak about his wicked son Antiochus Eupator. We will speak briefly about the many evils that occurred in the war.
When he succeeded to his father's kingdom, he placed Lysias in charge of his affairs, the man who had previously been made chief and governor over Syria and Phoenicia.
Ptolemy, who was called Macedon, maintained friendship with the Jews. He was distressed over the evils that had been done to them and wished to be at peace with them.

Some of his friends went and accused him before Eupator. They constantly called him a traitor because Philometor had entrusted Cyprus to him, but he had abandoned it and gone over to Antiochus Epiphanes. Because of this, he had neither high position nor honor in the kingdom. When he saw that all these things had happened to him, he took his own life with poison.
Gorgias took his place as chief and governor. He gathered many Gentiles around him and continually waged war against the Jews.
The Edomites also joined him. They came and attacked the fortresses near them and severely harassed the Jews. They welcomed those who fled from Jerusalem and prepared to wage war against Israel.
But Judas Maccabeus and his men cried out, prayed, and earnestly begged God to help them. Then they drew themselves up and advanced against the fortresses of the Edomites.
They fought against them mightily and bravely, exerted all their strength, and subdued them. They killed everyone who was fighting on the walls, killing about twenty thousand.
About nine thousand escaped from them and entered two large, strongly fortified strongholds.

Judas Maccabeus went to the places where he was needed, leaving Simon, Joseph, Zacchaeus, and many of his men to remain and fight against the strongholds and capture them. After Maccabeus left that place,

some of the men who were with Simon, because of their love of money, accepted bribes from those in the strongholds. They took seventy thousand pieces of silver from them and allowed some of them to escape.
When Maccabeus learned of the matter, he assembled the leaders of the people and rebuked them for selling their brothers for money and letting their enemies go.
He killed those who had acted as traitors and quickly captured the strongholds.
Although he had only a few men, he killed more than twenty thousand in their [?] strongholds.

Timothy, who had previously been defeated by the Jews, gathered a large and powerful foreign army, including the warriors of Asia and many cavalrymen. He advanced toward Jerusalem, intending to devastate Judea and take everyone in it captive.
When Maccabeus and his men heard that he was approaching, they devoted themselves to crying out and praying before God, with dust strewn on their heads and sackcloth tied around their waists.
They threw themselves down before the altar and asked the Lord to be reconciled to them, to help them, to fight against their enemies, and to stand against those who hated them, as the Law says.
When they had finished their prayers and petitions, they took up their weapons and advanced confidently against them. As they approached the battlefield, they grew quiet and kept to themselves.
When day broke and the sun rose, both sides began to fight. The Jews trusted in the Lord God, who had given them victory and deliverance, while the others trusted in the commanders of their army.
As the battle grew fierce and intense, five magnificent, glorious horsemen appeared from heaven to their enemies. Their horses were harnessed in gold, and they came to help the Jews.

They took Judas Maccabeus into their midst and sheltered him with the wings of their armor, protecting him from every blow. They hurled arrows and javelins at their enemies. When the enemies saw these things, their eyes were dazzled and all their strength gave way.
They killed twenty thousand five hundred of their infantry and six hundred cavalrymen.
Timothy fled to the stronghold called Gazara, which was exceedingly strong and well fortified. It was the prison of Chaereas, who had formerly been chief and governor there.
Maccabeus and his men confidently laid siege to the stronghold for four days.
Those inside, trusting in its strength and its fortifications, hurled outrageous insults and blasphemies at Judas Maccabeus and his men, speaking filthy and disgusting words to them.

As dawn approached on the fifth day, twenty young men who were with Maccabeus were filled with zeal and blazed with anger because of their blasphemy. They rushed against the stronghold, leaping forward bravely like raging wild beasts, and killed everyone who fell into their hands.

Others also leaped up and climbed the walls, setting fire to those in the towers. They kindled a fire and burned the blasphemers alive. Still others broke down the gates, and in this way they entered the city and captured it.
They found Timothy hiding in a pit and killed him there, along with his brother Chaereas and Apollonius.
After doing these things, they blessed God with praises and thanksgiving, because he had shown such great kindness to Israel and had given it victory.
A short time later, when Lysias, the king’s guardian and relative, heard about everything that had happened, he became angry and deeply embittered.
He gathered an army of more than eighty thousand, along with many cavalrymen, and advanced against the Jews, intending to make the city a dwelling place for Gentiles,
to make the temple a place for collecting money, like the other idol temples, and to dissolve and abolish the high priesthood.
He did not remember or keep before his eyes the greatness and judgment of God. Instead, he was proud and arrogant, trusting in the size of his army, his thousands of cavalrymen, and his elephants.
He entered Judea and advanced against Beth-zur. He encamped against a large village about ten thousand and five stadia from Jerusalem and began to besiege it.
When Maccabeus and his men heard that he had begun plundering and capturing fortresses, they begged the Lord with weeping and tears to send a good angel to save Israel.

Maccabeus himself was the first to take up his weapons. He urged and encouraged his companions to help their brothers who were suffering oppression from their enemies, and they all went forward together courageously.
While they were still near Jerusalem, their leader appeared to them in white clothing, riding a horse and wearing golden armor, flashing and brandishing his weapons toward them.
Immediately they all raised their voices and blessed the merciful God of heaven. They became firm and strong in spirit, ready not only to attack men but even to overthrow wild beasts and iron walls.
They went forward confidently, believing that God was merciful to them and was their helper.
They rushed upon their enemies like lions and struck down about eleven thousand of them, along with sixteen hundred cavalrymen. The rest fled.
Many of them, wounded, fled naked. Lysias himself also escaped by fleeing in great disgrace.
When Lysias came to his senses, he reflected on what had happened to him and concluded, saying, “The Hebrews cannot be defeated, because the mighty God is helping them.” So he sent word to them.
He sought to establish friendship with them and said that he would also persuade the king to be their friend.

Maccabeus agreed to everything Lysias requested, because he wanted the arrangements that would be helpful to take effect. The king granted the Jews everything that Maccabeus had written and sent to Lysias concerning them.
The letters that Lysias wrote to the Jews were as follows: “Lysias to the assembly of the Jews: Greetings.
“John and Absalom, whom you sent, delivered letters and made requests concerning what was written in them.
“I presented to the king what needed to be brought before him, and he granted what it was right to grant.
“If, then, you maintain your friendship with us, I will be the source of every benefit for you.
“Concerning the matters you wrote about, I have written and sent word that everything should be done for you as you wish.
“In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the twenty-fourth of Second Tishri.”
The king’s letter arrived, written as follows: “King Antiochus to his brother Lysias: Greetings.
“Since my father has gone to the gods, I wish our kingdom to be free from unrest. For this reason I have written concerning the care of the Jews.

For we have heard that they did not wish to submit to my father's intention of imposing paganism, but wanted to remain faithful to their own laws. For this reason they ask that their laws be left to them.
“We too wish this people to be free from unrest and fear, their temple to be restored to them, and their conduct and way of life to follow the laws and customs of their ancestors.
“You will therefore do well to send word to them and give them a pledge of peace, so that, when they see our goodwill toward them, they may go about all their affairs happily and peacefully.”
The king’s letter to the Jewish people was written as follows: “King Antiochus to the elders of the Jews and the rest of the Jews: Greetings.
“May you be in good health, as we wish. We too are well.
“Menelaus has informed us that you wish to go about your work and affairs peacefully and to live according to your laws.
“We too have given a pledge of peace and have pardoned offenses until the end of the month of Nisan.
“Let the Jews therefore live according to their laws as they did formerly, and let no one harass any of them over any matter whatsoever.
“I have sent Menelaus to inform you of these very things.”
Stay well. In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth of Nisan.
The Romans also sent a letter to the Jews, written as follows: “Quintus Memmius and Titus Manius, elders of the Romans, to the assembly of the Jews: Greetings.
We too approve of everything that Lysias, the king’s relative, has granted you.

Concerning everything else that he reported to the king about you, send men so that these matters may be settled for you and you may be satisfied in everything you desire, for we are about to go to Antioch.
Therefore hurry to send us someone who can inform us how you are doing.
In the year one hundred and forty-eight, on the fifteenth of Nisan.
When these matters had been settled, Lysias departed and went to the king, and the Jews returned to their farming and their work.
But the rulers and governors in the regions—Timothy, Apollonius son of Gennaeus, Hieronymus, Ramphon, and Nicanor—and the Cypriots with them would not let them have peace or rest.

The people of Joppa committed a great wickedness in this way: they persuaded the Jews living among them to board boats with their wives and children, although there was neither hostility nor conflict between them.

All the townspeople had planned this together and agreed to it, pretending that they wanted to act peacefully. Suspecting nothing, the Jews boarded and took their seats. Then the others went in and drowned them in the sea, about two hundred people.
When Judas heard about the evil and wickedness inflicted on his fellow Jews, he gave orders to the men with him.

He prayed and cried out to God, the righteous judge, and attacked those who had murdered their brothers. They burned their harbor at night, together with the ships in it, and killed those they found aboard them.

When the townspeople realized what was happening, they shut the gates. He turned back and went away, because he intended to attack them again and was planning to destroy Joppa along with its inhabitants.
He also learned that the people of Jamnia intended to do the same to the Jews living there.
He went there by night and burned their harbor with everything in it, so that the glow of the fire could be seen as far away as Jerusalem, two hundred and forty stadia away.
They traveled about nine stadia from there and were advancing against Timothy when Arabs attacked them, about five thousand infantry and five hundred cavalry.

When battle broke out and the fighting became fierce, Judas’s men were victorious because of the help God gave them. When the desert people were defeated, they asked Judas to give them a pledge of peace, promising also to give him pastureland.
Judas considered that they would be useful to him in many matters and agreed to make peace with them. After receiving his pledge, they went back to their tents.
Judas attacked a strong city, enclosed and fortified by its walls, in which people of many nations lived. Its name was Caspin.

Because its inhabitants trusted in the strength of their walls and the large supply of weapons stored inside, they were exceedingly arrogant. They blasphemed and insulted Judas’s men, speaking filthy and improper words to them.

Judas’s men prayed and cried out to God, the mighty Lord of the ages, who had overthrown the walls of Jericho in Joshua’s days without stones, siege engines, or human devices. They advanced and hurled themselves against the wall like wild animals, and tore it down.
By God’s will they captured the city and killed so many people in it that the nearby lake, about two stadia across, was entirely mingled with blood.
They departed from there and traveled about seven hundred and fifty stadia, entering Charax, where the Jews called Tobians lived.
They found Timothy in that region without strength and with his hands hanging helplessly, because he had no army with him. But he had left a garrison in a large, strong fortress.
Dositheus and Sosipater, commanders and leaders among the followers of Maccabeus, went and killed the men Timothy had left in the fortresses, more than ten thousand men.

Maccabeus gathered the army with him, divided them into units, and appointed a commander over each unit. He advanced against Timothy, who had come against them with a force of one hundred and twenty thousand infantry and two thousand five hundred cavalry.

When Timothy heard about Judas’s men, he sent their wives, children, and all their baggage to the town called Carnion. The town was rugged and fortified and could not easily be captured or plundered, because its approaches were narrow on every side.

When Judas’s advance force appeared, fear and trembling fell upon the enemies by the will of God, the ruler of all, who appeared to them. They all took to flight, each fleeing in his own direction. As they ran and climbed over one another, they collided and wounded one another’s limbs, because their swords were drawn.
Judas pursued them fiercely, killing those wicked men. He killed about thirty thousand of them.

Timothy himself fell into the hands of the men of Dositheus and Sosipater, who captured him. He begged and pleaded with them to spare his life. Now many of them had brothers and relatives in his custody.
He promised them that he would release those men alive. For the sake of their brothers’ lives, they felt constrained to yield to him and let him live.
Then Judas Maccabeus marched against the place called Carna and Atargatis and killed twenty-five thousand there.

After these people had been defeated and killed, Judas rallied his army and marched against Ephron, a fortified city where Lysias lived, together with a large gathering of Gentiles and strong young men. They fought fiercely from its walls with arrows, javelins, and every kind of weapon.

Judas and his men prayed and cried out to God, who has the power to crush and shatter all the strength of their enemies. He delivered the city into their hands, and they entered, captured it, and killed about twenty-five thousand in it.
From there they set out and went to Beth-shan, which is about six hundred stadia from Jerusalem.
The Jews who lived there spoke appreciatively of the city's inhabitants, saying that they treated them very kindly and respected them.
Judas and his men acknowledged their kindness and greeted them peacefully. From there they went to Jerusalem to celebrate the Festival of Unleavened Bread.
After Pentecost they marched against Gorgias, the ruler and governor of the Idumeans.
He came out against them with three thousand infantry and four hundred cavalry.
When they began fighting, a few men among the Idumeans fell.

Dositheus, one of the Tobians, a cavalryman and a mighty warrior, seized Gorgias by his cloak and forcibly dragged him along, because he wanted to bring the guilty man in alive. But one of Gorgias's soldiers, a Thracian, confronted him, struck him on the shoulder, and cut it off. Gorgias escaped and went to Samaria.
Azariah's men were fighting very fiercely and killing. Judas cried out to the mighty Lord to help them, and he himself led the attack against the enemy.
While he was singing hymns in the voice of the ancestors, he began killing them. Gorgias and his men were defeated and fled.
Judas and his army set out from there and came to the city of Adullam. As the Sabbath approached, they purified themselves according to their custom and observed the Sabbath where they were.
The next day they came to Judas and asked him to let them take the bodies of those who had fallen and bury them in their ancestral tombs.

Under the clothes of each of them they found hidden gold from the idols of Jamnia, things that the law commanded the Jews not to keep for themselves. Everyone understood and became convinced that this was why these men had fallen.
They all blessed God and gave thanks for his righteous judgment, for he brings hidden things out and reveals them openly.

They all began to pray and plead with God that a deadly sin would not be charged against them because of this. The valiant Judas urged and implored all the people to guard themselves and beware of sins. He told them, "Look, you have seen with your own eyes what happened to these men."

He required all the people to contribute silver, collected three thousand pieces of silver, and sent it to Jerusalem so that sacrifices could be offered on their behalf. He acted justly and rightly because of his hope in the resurrection from the dead.
For if he had not been expecting and hoping for the resurrection from the dead, it would have been pointless and foolish for anyone to pray and offer sacrifices on behalf of the dead.

For he was looking forward to and awaiting the reward, hope, and rest prepared for those who die in righteousness. That is why he sent the money, so that atonement might be made for the sins of those who had died.
In the one hundred and forty-ninth year, Antiochus Eupator came against the Jews.

With him was Lysias, who had been put in charge of affairs. He had an army drawn from many nations: one hundred and ten thousand infantry, five thousand three hundred cavalry, twenty-two elephants, and three hundred chariots equipped with shields for battle.

Menelaus also went and joined them. He begged and pleaded with Antiochus to march against his country and his fellow citizens to destroy them, not to help them, because he expected to go and assume leadership.

But the Lord, the King of kings, stirred up Antiochus's anger against the guilty Menelaus, because Lysias had informed him that Menelaus was the cause of all the troubles. He ordered them to take him to Aleppo and put him to death there.
There was a tower there, fifty cubits high, filled with ashes. It had wheels and was moved by a mechanism.
There they confined the plunderer of the temple, the perpetrator of all these evils.
The guilty and wicked Menelaus died in this torment and was not considered worthy even of burial in the earth. He justly received his punishment.
Because he had committed evil acts against the altar, where the holy fire and ashes were, he met his death in ashes.
The king was still angry and bitterly hostile toward the Jews, and he was planning to inflict many more evils on them than his father had.

But the king’s arrival and plans were revealed to Judas. He commanded the people to remain watchful in prayer day and night and to cry out to God to help them and deliver them, now and always, from the hands of the nations,

who wanted to drive them away from the law, their country, and the holy temple. They were also to ask him not to allow the people, who had enjoyed relief and rest for only a short time, to be enslaved to wicked and uncircumcised nations.

They all prayed and cried out in this way, pleading with the merciful God with many tears while fasting for three days. They continually lay facedown and cried out. After three days Judas appealed to them and encouraged them to eat.
