Judas went alone to the elders and consulted with them. He said, “Before the king’s army enters Judea and they conquer the city and exhaust its strength, let us go out, take action, and put everything in order with God’s help.”

He placed the leadership in the hands of God, the Creator of the world, and urged those with him to fight bravely and surrender their lives, even to death, for the law, the temple, the city, the country, and their fellow people. He gathered his entire army, and they made preparations at Modein [?].

He gave those with him the watchword, “God’s salvation,” and took selected, strong young men with him. He went against the camp and attacked the king’s courtyard at night. There he killed about three thousand men, and crushed and brought down the largest of the elephants, together with all its equipment.
They filled the whole camp with terror and confusion, and returned from there with delight and joy.
They did this as dawn was approaching, because the Lord’s power and help were overshadowing them.
When the king had experienced and seen the Jews’ strength and courage, he wanted to subdue them through skill and deceit.
He sent a force against Beth-zur, the Jews’ stronghold. They fought against it, but were defeated and suffered heavy losses.
Meanwhile, Judas kept sending supplies to those inside the fortresses.
Rhodocus went from the land of Judea and disclosed their secret to their enemies. Judas gave orders, and they found him and killed him.
The king came against Beth-zur again, exchanged pledges, and departed.

He went against Judas and his men and fought with them, but was defeated and withdrew. He suspected that Philip, whom he had appointed to oversee affairs in Antioch, wanted to rebel against him. He therefore agreed to make peace with the Jews, put himself under obligation to them, swore an oath to them, and established friendship with them. He offered sacrifices and greatly honored the temple, and also showed kindness toward the country.
He received Maccabeus with great affection and left Hegemonides as chief and governor from Ptolemais as far as Gazara.
He went to Ptolemais. The people of Ptolemais were upset about the agreement he had made with the Jews. They were extremely angry with him and wanted to dissolve the agreement he had made with them.
Lysias came forward before the tribunal, gave them relief, persuaded them, and calmed them. Then he departed from there for Antioch. Such was the king’s journey and arrival.
After three years, Demetrius son of Seleucus came against Judas and his men. He entered the harbor of Alas with a large, powerful, and heavily armed army.
To take possession of the whole land, because he had killed Antiochus and Lysias, his chief steward.

Alcimus, who had previously been high priest but had thoroughly defiled himself during the times of intermingling, considered his situation and saw that he had no hope at all and could not even approach the altar.

He went to King Demetrius in the year one hundred and fifty-one and brought him a gold crown, a gold ear of grain, and palm branches from the temple along with them. That day, however, he remained quiet.

When Alcimus found an opportunity for his audacity and wrongdoing, Demetrius summoned him to the council and asked him, “With what intention or plan are the Jews strengthening themselves in this way?” He answered him:

“Those who are called the distinguished men among the Jews, over whom Judas Maccabeus has been appointed, are rebelling, stirring up trouble, and intensifying the war. They do not allow the kingdom to enjoy peace.
For this reason I too have left behind the glory of my ancestors, which is the high priesthood, and now I have come before you for the second time.

I do so because I care about the king’s affairs and bear responsibility for them, and secondly because of our own people. For I see the arrogance and pride of those I mentioned earlier, how they oppress our people and do not allow them even a little rest.”
But now, O king, since you have learned these things, take up the cause of our land and our afflicted and wretched people, in keeping with your compassion toward all humanity.
For as long as Judas lives, there can be no peace in our land.
When the king heard these words from him, the king’s friends, who were hostile to Judas, immediately inflamed Demetrius’s anger against him.
Immediately King Demetrius summoned Nicanor, who had been appointed commander over the elephants, a ruler and governor.
He gave him letters and sent him off, ordering him to put Judas to death, scatter those who were with him, and install Alcimus as high priest of the great and glorious temple.
The Gentiles who had fled from the land of Judea came and joined Nicanor. They delighted and rejoiced in the distress and trouble facing Judas and his followers.

When Judas and his followers heard about Nicanor’s coming and the hostility of the Gentiles, they put dust on their heads and cried out, praying before the one who had always been their helper and had always openly delivered his inheritance.
Judas ordered them to equip themselves with their weapons, and they immediately set out and met them at a village called Dessau.
Simon, Judas’s brother, had made a sudden attack on Nicanor, but because they advanced against him hastily, they were frightened by him.

Nicanor, however, had heard about the bravery of Judas and his followers, their victories, and how they gave up their lives for their people and their country. He did not want to settle the matter through slaughter and bloodshed.
Instead, he sent Posidonius, Theodotus, and Mattathias to exchange pledges of friendship.
When Judas heard this, he consulted with the people. They considered the matter together, saw that Nicanor’s words were peaceful, and agreed to make peace with him.
They agreed on a day to meet one another. Each of them was surrounded by armed men [?].

Judas ordered his army to equip themselves with their weapons. They stood ready at the places where they feared some treachery might suddenly occur. The two men met on very friendly terms and spoke words of peace.
Nicanor stayed in Jerusalem and did nothing wrong. He dismissed the Gentiles who had gathered around him.
He held Judas in great affection and was always cheerful in his company.
He asked him and persuaded him to marry and have children. So Judas married and took part in ordinary life.

When Alcimus saw the affection and harmony between Nicanor and Judas, he went to King Demetrius and told him about Nicanor: “He has become disloyal to your kingdom and to all your affairs, for he has made Judas, who is an enemy of your kingdom, his partner and friend.”

When the king heard the enemy’s slander, he became furiously angry and wrote harshly to Nicanor about his friendship with Judas. He ordered him to seize Maccabeus, bind him, and send him quickly to Antioch.
When Nicanor heard the letter, he was disheartened and deeply distressed. He did not want to change his attitude toward Judas, a man who had done nothing wrong.
Yet he could not defy the king’s command, and he considered what pretext he could use to arrest him.

When Maccabeus saw that Nicanor’s expression toward him was no longer as it had been before, but was gloomy and different from usual, he realized that Nicanor’s attitude toward him had indeed changed. He gathered a considerable number of his countrymen around him and withdrew from Nicanor.

When Nicanor learned that Judas had prepared himself and strengthened his forces, he entered the great and holy temple while the priests were standing and offering sacrifices. He said to them, “Hand Judas over to me.”
But they swore to him, saying, “We have not seen him, and we do not know where he is.”

He raised his hand toward the temple and swore to them: “Unless you hand Judas over in chains, I will turn this temple of God into a wasteland, tear down the altar, and build a distinguished temple to Dionysus in its place.”
After saying all this, he left. The priests stretched out their hands toward the one who dwells in heaven. They pleaded and prayed to the one who had always been his people’s helper, saying:
You are the Lord of all, and you need nothing. You chose to select a place for your temple, so that your presence might dwell among us.
“And now, Lord, holiest of all holy ones, preserve forever this place and this undefiled house, which has recently been purified, and shut every mouth of the unjust.”

A man named Razis, one of the elders of Jerusalem, was reported to Nicanor as a man who loved his city and had an excellent reputation. Because of his good and kindly disposition, he was called the father of the Jews.
For he had previously been on trial, and he had not allowed any intermingling among the Jewish people. His soul and body were devoted, with every prayer and petition, to the practices of Judaism.
Nicanor, wanting to make known the hatred he had for the Jews, sent about five hundred of his soldiers to arrest him.
For he said, “When I arrest this man, I will cause the Jews great distress.”

When the crowd arrived and surrounded his courtyard, they tried to break open the gates and burn them with fire. When he saw that they were close to arresting him, he took a sword and struck himself in the belly.
For he wanted to die as a free man rather than be handed over to wicked and unjust men who would disgrace the dignity of his old age.

His blow failed because of his haste and agitation. When the crowds entered through the courtyard gates, he sprang up onto the wall bravely and forcefully and threw himself into the middle of the crowds.
When they saw this, they immediately drew back and made room.

While he was still alive and burning with fierce zeal, he leaped up and stood, though much blood was flowing from him because his wounds were severe. He ran through the entire crowd and stood on a high rock.

He was covered all over with blood. He pulled out his intestines, held them in both hands, and showed them to the people. He prayed and pleaded, calling on the one who has authority over life and spirit to give them back to him and restore them again. Then he departed from this world.
Nicanor heard and learned that Judas and his men were near Samaria, and he planned to attack them unexpectedly with a large force on the Sabbath day of rest.

The Jews pleaded with him in great distress, saying, “Do not do this and cruelly destroy people who do not deserve it. Instead, give honor to the great and holy day that is honored by the Maker and Creator of all.”
But the wicked and impure man asked whether there was a mighty one in heaven who had given the command concerning the Sabbath day.
They answered him, “There is the living Lord. He is the mighty one in heaven, and he commanded that the Sabbath day be observed.”
The impure and wicked man answered, “I too am mighty on earth, and I command you to take up arms and carry out the king’s business.” He did not refrain from carrying out his impure plan.
Nicanor was puffed up and exalted himself with great arrogance. He learned that Judas and his men were gathered and ready, and he became still more aggressive.
But Judas Maccabeus was hopeful and fully confident that God would bring him deliverance.

He encouraged those with him and told them not to fear the crowds of nations coming against them. He reminded them again of the help they had received from heaven in the past, saying, “Look and wait for the victory that will come to you from God, the ruler of all.”
He exhorted them from the Law and the Prophets and reminded them of the heroic deeds and struggles they had undertaken in the past. He strengthened them and gave them courage.
He stirred up anger and zeal in them, also showing them the wickedness of the nations and the treachery with which they had broken their oath.

Judas armed and equipped each of them, not with spears and shields, but with good words of comfort, encouragement, and strength. He told them about a vision he had seen that deserved to be accepted and believed. When they heard it, they were all heartened.

This was the account of the vision he had seen: he saw Onias the priest, who had been a noble and good man, modest in his [?], humble by nature, and pleasant and gracious in his speech. From his youth he had followed everything that was right and fitting for the covenant. He saw this man in the vision with his hands stretched out, praying for the entire Jewish people.
Afterward, another man appeared to him, distinguished by a beautiful old age and great glory. His appearance was outstanding, and he bore a majestic beauty.
Onias answered and said about him, “This is Jeremiah the prophet, who loves his brothers and earnestly pleads, makes supplication, and prays for the people and the holy city.”
Jeremiah stretched out his right hand, gave Judas a golden spear, and said to him,
“Receive this spear, a gift from God, with which you will strike and crush all your enemies.”

When Judas’s companions heard these words, they were comforted by his fine words and greatly strengthened. For his words could strengthen, uplift, and fortify those who heard them, and bring the young men’s spirits to perfection. They resolved not to rely on battle formations and preparations, but to stand firm with all courage and willingly expose themselves to hardship, fully resolved to defend the holy city, the holy temple, and the entire sanctuary.
For they were less concerned about their wives, children, brothers, and families. Their great anxiety and concern were for the holy temple.
Those who had remained in the city also faced no small struggle and distress, fearing that they might become frightened and lose heart amid the turmoil of battle.

While they were all awaiting the coming decision, the enemy advanced, drew up their ranks opposite them, and made ready. The elephants took their places in the ranks, and the cavalry also armed themselves and stood at their posts.

When Judas Maccabeus saw their ranks, the strength of the enemy army, their stock of weapons, and the readiness and ferocity of the elephants, he raised his hands to heaven, prayed, and cried out to God, who performs wonders and mighty deeds. For he knew that victory in battle did not depend on weapons, but that God gave victory to whomever he wished.
As he prayed and pleaded, he said: “You, Lord, sent your angel in the days of Hezekiah king of Judah, and he killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand in Sennacherib’s camp.
“Now, mighty one who dwells in heaven, send a good angel before us, and let him cast trembling, terror, and panic upon them.
“By the strength and greatness of your arm, let those who have come blasphemously against your holy people fall.” Judas concluded with these words.
Nicanor’s men advanced to battle with lyres, harps, and the music of horns.
But Judas’s men charged against them with prayer and supplication.

They fought with their hands while praying in their hearts and crying out to God. They struck down and killed about thirty-five thousand of them, and they rejoiced and exulted in the help God had given them.
When they had stopped fighting and returned from battle, rejoicing, giving thanks, and praising God, they learned that Nicanor had fallen in battle along with all the soldiers who accompanied him.
There was turmoil and panic in his camp. But Judas and his men gave thanks and blessed the Lord in the language of their ancestors.

Then the man who had devoted himself, body and soul, to every hardship for the sake of his people and his city, and who had gladly served all his days as his people’s leader and commander in battle, ordered them to cut off Nicanor’s head and his arm at the shoulder and bring them to Jerusalem.
When Maccabeus came to Jerusalem, he summoned his people and the priests before the altar, and sent for the men of the citadel.
He showed them the head of the impure Nicanor and the blasphemer’s arm, which he had raised in pride and arrogance against the temple of God, the ruler of all.
He cut the wicked man’s tongue out of his head, cut it into small pieces, and ordered that it be given to the birds. He nailed up his hand opposite the temple.
Then they all blessed the Lord who dwells in heaven, crying out, “Praised are you, Lord, who have kept your place pure!”
He fastened the impure man’s head in a high and conspicuous place opposite the citadel, so that everyone could see it and know the deliverance brought by our God.

They agreed among themselves not to let this day pass as an ordinary day, but to mark this day, the thirteenth of Adar, the twelfth month. In the Aramaic language it is described as one day before Mordecai’s day.

This is how things happened concerning Nicanor and everything that took place in those days. From that time onward, the Hebrews held and governed their cities. And now I will bring my account to an end.
If it has been composed well and skillfully, that is what I myself desired. But if it is inadequate and poor, may I be forgiven for this.

For just as drinking wine alone or water alone gives no pleasure to the soul, while wine mixed with water is pleasant and gives its full benefit to those who drink it, so the arrangement and composition of an account gladden and delight the ears of those who read, study attentively, examine, and investigate it. So let this now be the conclusion of the historical account.
